prompt: Each company below splits its market in one way. Is it segmenting geographically or demographically?

cards.text: A tire maker sells snow tires in Québec and all-season tires in British Columbia.
cards.explanation: Québec and British Columbia are geographical units (provinces), so the market is divided by place.

cards.text: A bank offers one account for university students and another for retirees.
cards.explanation: Students and retirees differ in age and life-cycle stage, which are demographic variables.

cards.text: A coffee chain changes its menu for each Montréal neighborhood, from the Plateau to Saint-Laurent.
cards.explanation: Neighborhoods are a geographical unit, so this is geographic segmentation.

cards.text: A travel company designs one tour for baby boomers and a different one for Gen Z.
cards.explanation: Baby boomers and Gen Z are generations, one of the demographic variables.

cards.text: A car brand aims its top model at households earning over $250,000 a year.
cards.explanation: The company divides buyers by income, a demographic variable.

cards.text: A phone company runs one plan for big cities and another for rural counties.
cards.explanation: Cities and counties are geographical units, so this is geographic segmentation.

prompt: A fitness and sportswear brand segments its buyers using psychographic and behavioral variables. Which variable is it using in each case?

cases.text: It designs a minimalist apparel line for buyers who value slow, mindful living and holistic wellness, even though they share the same income bracket as competitive gym-goers.
cases.explanation: Mindful living and competitive fitness reflect lifestyle and personality traits rather than demographics or product usage.

cases.text: It runs a campaign in the weeks before the Montréal marathon, when runners buy new shoes.
cases.explanation: The campaign is timed to a specific event when buyers get the idea to buy or use the item.

cases.text: It sells one shoe line to buyers who want joint-protecting cushioning and another to buyers who want race-day speed.
cases.explanation: Cushioning and speed are the specific functional benefits buyers desire from the product.

cases.text: It sends a starter guide and trial voucher to people who have never bought running gear before.
cases.explanation: Distinguishing nonusers and first-time users from regular users segments the market by user status.

cases.text: It offers a volume bundle to heavy runners who wear out three pairs of shoes a year.
cases.explanation: Grouping light, medium, and heavy users divides buyers by usage rate.

cases.text: It invites customers who have bought only its brand for five years to a private preview sale.
cases.explanation: Grouping buyers by how consistently they choose the brand over rivals segments by loyalty status.

prompt: A B2B software firm is testing five proposed market segments. Each proposal fails one of the five requirements for effective segmentation. Which requirement does each fail?

cases.text: Segmenting procurement managers by whether they privately feel impostor syndrome during contract renewals, a trait no survey or database can estimate.
cases.explanation: If the size, purchasing power, and profile of the group cannot be measured, the segment fails the measurable criterion.

cases.text: Targeting independent fishing crews who spend ten months at sea with no internet, trade press, or port brokers through which a sales team could reach them.
cases.explanation: When a firm has no effective channel to reach and serve the buyers, the segment fails the accessible criterion.

cases.text: Building a custom enterprise accounting suite for a niche that contains only four small workshops nationwide.
cases.explanation: A segment that is too small to cover the cost of a tailored program fails the substantial criterion.

cases.text: Splitting mid-size law firms and mid-size accounting firms into separate segments even though both buy the exact same plan and respond identically to price and features.
cases.explanation: If two groups respond the same way to every marketing mix element, they are not differentiable segments.

cases.text: Identifying seven distinct global industry segments when the startup has only two salespeople and no budget to design separate programs for them.
cases.explanation: If the company lacks the capability to design effective programs to attract and serve the segments, they are not actionable.

prompt: Each company below has chosen a market coverage strategy along the targeting continuum. Which strategy is it using?

cases.text: A staple commodity producer sells a single standard box of iodized table salt with the same price and advertising to every household in the country.
cases.explanation: Going after the whole market with one uniform offer that focuses on common needs is undifferentiated (mass) marketing.

cases.text: An eyewear corporation operates three distinct retail chains: a budget frame shop, a mid-priced family optical store, and a luxury designer boutique.
cases.explanation: Targeting several distinct segments and designing separate offers and brands for each is differentiated marketing.

cases.text: A small instrument workshop builds and markets guitars exclusively for left-handed jazz musicians.
cases.explanation: Pursuing a large share of one narrow, specialized segment is concentrated (niche) marketing.

cases.text: A footwear company uses a 3D foot scan from a customer's phone to print a pair of insoles shaped to that individual's exact arch.
cases.explanation: Tailoring products to the exact needs of individual customers is individual marketing, a form of micromarketing.

cases.text: A supermarket chain stocks Caribbean groceries in its downtown Toronto stores and Korean groceries in its North York stores based on neighborhood demographics.
cases.explanation: Tailoring assortments to specific cities or neighborhoods is local marketing, part of micromarketing.

prompt: A laptop maker is choosing which differences to promote. Each difference below fails one of the seven criteria. Which one?

cases.text: The logo on the lid comes in 40 colors, but target buyers say they do not care about it.
cases.explanation: A difference must deliver a highly valued benefit to target buyers. This one does not matter to them.

cases.text: Its laptops charge through USB-C, just like every other laptop on the shelf.
cases.explanation: Competitors already offer the same feature in the same way, so it is not distinctive.

cases.text: It claims fast wake-from-sleep, but a rival's laptop wakes up twice as fast.
cases.explanation: Customers can obtain the same benefit more effectively from another brand, so the difference is not superior.

cases.text: An internal voltage regulator slightly extends motherboard life, but buyers cannot see, feel, or verify what it does.
cases.explanation: If buyers cannot perceive or understand the difference, it fails the communicable test.

cases.text: Its new keyboard shortcut layout can be copied by any competitor in a software update within two weeks.
cases.explanation: Competitors can copy the feature easily, so the difference is not preemptive.

cases.text: A solid-titanium hinge is durable, but it adds $900 to the price of a student laptop.
cases.explanation: Target buyers cannot afford to pay the added cost of the difference, so it fails the affordable test.

cases.text: Unlimited free accidental-damage replacements would cost the company more than its margin on each laptop.
cases.explanation: The company cannot introduce the difference profitably, so it fails the profitable test.

prompt: Compare each brand with its rivals. Match each winning value proposition to the brand strategy that illustrates it.

pairs.match: A luxury hotel provides private butlers, bespoke suites, and Michelin-starred dining, and charges three times the nightly rate of standard hotels.
pairs.explanation: Providing upscale benefits at a correspondingly high price is More for More.

pairs.match: An automaker launches a sedan with quieter cabin insulation and a longer powertrain warranty than established luxury rivals while matching their mid-tier price.
pairs.explanation: Offering higher quality or more benefits at a price comparable to rivals is More for the Same.

pairs.match: A warehouse club sells leading national-brand electronics and pantry staples at a 25% discount through high-volume purchasing and low-cost store operations.
pairs.explanation: Offering standard benefits and quality at a deep discount is The Same for Less.

pairs.match: A budget carrier removes complimentary meals, seat selection, and checked baggage to sell flights at a fraction of full-service airline fares.
pairs.explanation: Meeting lower frill requirements at rock-bottom prices is Less for Much Less.

pairs.match: A new hardware chain opens with a wider tool selection, free workshops, and lower prices than every local rival, a combination that is powerful at launch but hard to sustain.
pairs.explanation: Offering more benefits while charging less is More for Less.

question_text: A commuter backpack brand spends heavily on cinematic video ads with the tagline "Move Without Limits." However, when urban cyclists ask conversational AI assistants for "waterproof commuter backpacks that fit a 16-inch laptop under $150," the brand never appears in the three-brand shortlist. Based on how AI assistants construct consideration sets, what is the primary positioning failure?
hint: Consider what sources a conversational AI assistant synthesizes when translating a need-based prompt into a shortlist.
correct_answer_citation: Positioning in an AI-mediated market therefore means linking the brand name consistently to specific target segments, usage occasions, and verifiable points of difference across all public text and catalog data.

options.option_text: The brand has not linked its name consistently to target segments, usage occasions, and verifiable attribute facts across public product pages, reviews, and comparison articles.
options.option_explanation: Correct. AI assistants synthesize structured product specifications, independent review sites, and comparison articles to match a user's prompt constraints. Without verifiable public text linking the brand to urban cycling, waterproofing, and laptop capacity, the brand is omitted from the shortlist.

options.option_text: Conversational AI assistants recommend only brands that follow a Less for Much Less value proposition.
options.option_explanation: AI assistants match the specific constraints and benefits stated in the user's prompt rather than restricting results to rock-bottom budget brands.

options.option_text: The brand used demographic segmentation instead of undifferentiated mass marketing in its video campaign.
options.option_explanation: The issue is not that the brand targeted a segment, but that its public text and catalog data lack the concrete, verifiable facts needed for the AI assistant to match the brand to that segment's query.

options.option_text: Television and video commercials automatically disqualify a brand from being indexed by product review websites.
options.option_explanation: Memorable image advertising does not disqualify a brand, but image ads alone cannot substitute for structured specifications and third-party review evidence that AI assistants read.
